column5: just balances belong to the Lord
column6: The commentary treats a short measure as a concrete market loss; Proverbs says just balances and weights belong to the Lord. This adds divine ownership to the duty of accurate trade.

column5: God weighs the speaker in just scales
column6: The commentary joins deficient scales to a final account; Job asks to be weighed in a just balance so God may know his integrity. The verse brings commercial measurement into divine judgment.

column5: wealth lost in a bad venture
column6: The commentary describes trade consuming its principal; Ecclesiastes says wealth can be lost in a bad venture, leaving a father with nothing to pass on. It gives the loss of capital a concrete household consequence.

column5: nothing carried away from toil
column6: The commentary says accumulated wealth cannot outlast a person's time; Ecclesiastes says a person leaves as naked as at birth and takes nothing from toil. It makes the final loss bodily and irreversible.

column5: wealth takes wings
column6: The commentary rejects the belief that wealth can secure a person's future; Proverbs says wealth can suddenly make wings and fly away. It adds an image of capital disappearing beyond its owner's control.

column5: riches fail on the day of wrath
column6: The commentary contrasts a losing trade with the righteous path; Proverbs says riches do not profit on the day of wrath, while righteousness delivers from death. It directly contrasts wealth with the return of right conduct.

column5: remember the creator before difficult days
column6: The commentary says a late plea for more time comes after the market has closed; Ecclesiastes urges remembering the creator in youth before the difficult days arrive. It makes the timing of good action urgent.

column5: faithfulness with money and true riches
column6: The commentary sets trust against betrayal in a commercial setting; Jesus says that failure to be faithful with unrighteous wealth means no one will entrust true riches. It makes money management a test of trustworthiness.

column5: God and wealth as rival masters
column6: The commentary frames the righteous trade as choosing the lasting good over a losing exchange; Jesus says a person cannot serve both God and mammon. It makes wealth a question of allegiance, not merely its amount.

column5: money placed with bankers for interest
column6: The commentary describes capital invested for gain; in the talents parable the master says the servant should have placed the money with bankers so it could return with interest. It makes the expected return explicit.

column5: faithful servant receives greater charge
column6: The commentary connects faithful work to a wage; the master praises a servant faithful over a little, entrusts him with much, and invites him into joy. It adds increased responsibility as the reward for stewardship.

column5: agreed denarius as a worker's due
column6: The commentary says a wage is an obligation once due; the vineyard owner answers a complaint by pointing to the agreed denarius. This gives the parable's wage a contractual basis alongside its generosity to later workers.

column5: faithful through death, crowned with life
column6: The commentary couples patience with a wage at the end of the worker's time; Revelation tells Smyrna to remain faithful even to death and promises the crown of life. It makes endurance under threat part of the reward image.

column5: selling goods to give alms and store unfailing treasure
column6: The commentary presents a trade whose return does not fail and recalls a plea for time to give charity; Jesus tells hearers to sell possessions, give to the poor, and provide an unfailing heavenly treasure. It makes generosity a deliberate transfer from perishable wealth.

column5: lending to the Lord by helping the poor
column6: The commentary says God is the buyer and guarantor of a promised return; Proverbs says whoever is generous to the poor lends to the Lord, who repays the giver. It casts care for the poor as a loan whose return comes from God.

column5: repayment at the resurrection
column6: The commentary links righteous deeds to a later wage; Jesus says a host who invites the poor, disabled, lame, and blind will be repaid at the resurrection of the righteous. It specifies generosity that cannot be repaid in the present market.

column5: service to the least counted as service to the king
column6: The commentary says mutual counsel must recognize another person's due; in the judgment scene the king identifies care for the least of his siblings as care for himself. It gives acts of service a direct relation to the final judge.

column5: alms stored as treasure for a future day
column6: The commentary contrasts wealth that perishes with a trade that does not fail; Tobit says alms lay up a good treasure for the day of need. It makes generosity a future-oriented deposit.

column5: others receive the wealth the hoarder prepared
column6: The commentary says wealth cannot outlast its owner; Job says the righteous will wear the garments the wicked prepared and the innocent will divide the silver. This neighboring verse makes the transfer of accumulated wealth explicit.

column5: God rewards those who seek him
column6: The commentary makes belief one condition of escaping loss and describes a later wage; Hebrews says faith is necessary to approach God and that God rewards those who seek him. It joins faith to expected recompense.

column5: fixed times for Torah study at judgment
column6: The commentary treats a person's time as capital that must be spent before the account closes; Shabbat 31a asks at judgment whether one fixed times for Torah study. This adds deliberate use of time to the passage's separate question about honest business.

column5: shared support keeps hands steady until sunset
column6: The commentary joins mutual urging to patience with the end of the workday; Aaron and Hur support Moses' hands until sunset so they remain steady. The scene adds physical, shared endurance through the day's limit.

column5: Arabic root ء م ن; package table's unverified sound correspondence to Hebrew אמנ
column6: The commentary glosses amānah as trust opposed to betrayal; Deuteronomy calls God faithful and without injustice. This Hebrew use joins fidelity to justice, though the root correspondence remains unverified.

column5: Arabic root خ س ر; package table's unverified sound correspondence to Hebrew חסר
column6: The commentary defines loss through diminution and deficiency; Deuteronomy commands opening a hand to a poor person for whatever he lacks (חסר). It connects lack to a neighbor's material need, though cognacy is unverified.

column5: Arabic root ص ب ر; package table's unverified sound correspondence to Hebrew צבר
column6: The commentary's Arabic lexical branch calls a ṣubrah a heap sold without weighing; the psalm uses צבר for heaping up wealth and says the person does not know who will gather it. The heap becomes a warning about wealth outliving its owner; cognacy is unverified.

column5: Arabic root ص ب ر; package table's unverified sound correspondence to Hebrew צבר
column6: The commentary's lexical branch connects ṣubrah with a heap; Job says the wicked may heap up silver like dust. The shared heap image is specific, while the sound correspondence remains unverified.

column5: Arabic root ء م ن; package table's unverified sound correspondence to Hebrew אמנ
column6: The commentary's Arabic lexical gloss associates amānah with trust and firmness; Exodus describes Moses' hands as steady (emunah) until sunset. The Hebrew usage gives the root a bodily sense of sustained firmness, but the sound correspondence is unverified.
